Marvell has surged 214% in 2026 while Broadcom has gained just 3%, after raising its custom AI silicon forecast to tens of billions in revenue.

NVIDIA is up 22% and SOXX up 79% in 2026, but Marvell's concentrated customer base means one lost design win could sharply reverse those gains.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Broadcom didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat AVGO. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

One custom chip designer has more than doubled in value this year so far. Shares of Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) are trading at $266.27, up 214% year to date.

gorodenkoff / Getty Images

Chip stocks more broadly have also climbed, though at a slower pace. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), which counts Marvell among its holdings, is up 79% year to date. Tech's wider benchmark, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), is up 21% year to date.

Meanwhile, shares of Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO), the larger custom silicon rival, are at $356.16, up 3% year to date, a fraction of Marvell stock's advance. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock is at $227.18, up 22% year to date, also far short of the custom chip designer's pace.

Investor Day Puts Custom Silicon Center Stage

Marvell held its investor day in early October and used it to press the case for its custom artificial intelligence (AI) silicon business. That unit designs application-specific chips for individual hyperscale customers, with each part built around one buyer's workloads. In the same week, Marvell raised its forecast for the custom business and set out a long-range revenue ambition reaching into the tens of billions of dollars.

At an industry hardware summit in October, Marvell also showed a new high-capacity data center switch. The switch extends the company's reach in networking and connectivity, the components that link AI chips together inside a cluster.

Three Business Models Price One AI Buildout

Marvell builds custom silicon along with data center networking and connectivity components for a small number of very large customers, and a single design win can carry years of revenue while losing one has the same weight in reverse. This structure helps explain why Marvell stock can swing harder than the broader chip group when its customer pipeline shifts.

Broadcom runs the same custom accelerator model at far greater scale and pairs it with a large enterprise software business, while NVIDIA, for its part, sells general-purpose graphics processors into the merchant market, where many customers buy the same part.

Contracted Demand Versus Priced-In Execution

Supporters could argue that custom accelerator demand is contracted years ahead and that Marvell has only recently been credited for it. Hyperscale buyers commit to a design long before volume production begins, so visibility in this model can stretch well past an ordinary chip cycle.

A run of this magnitude prices in execution Marvell hasn't yet delivered, the skeptics argue. Customer concentration sharpens that risk, since one lost socket could undo a great deal of the gain.

What to Watch Next

Marvell's unresolved question is whether the custom silicon revenue it has guided toward arrives on the schedule its valuation now assumes. Shareholders can watch for whether program ramps tied to the raised custom forecast begin to show up in the company's upcoming reports. Orders for the new data center switch could also indicate how quickly the networking side turns product launches into revenue.

A rally this steep can reverse quickly. This could happen if a concentrated customer base changes its plans, and the traits that showed up years before the biggest tech runs are the ones we cataloged in a free guide here: The Next NVIDIA Playbook. Investors should size their MRVL share positions so that a single lost design win wouldn't ruin their portfolio. Those weighing whether to take profits may want to keep an eye on whether Broadcom and NVIDIA shares begin to narrow the gap with Marvell stock.

title: Why Money Market Funds Are So Popular

Why Money Market Funds Are So Popular
Neena Mishra

Explore stocks on Coinbase

US money market funds gathered more than $166 billion in the week ending October 7, 2026, according to Bank of America, marking their largest inflows since April 2020. Assets in money market funds have now topped $8 trillion, as these products remain popular with both institutional and retail investors due to their low risk and attractive short-term interest rates.

With the Federal Reserve expected to raise rates several times in the coming months, investors are preferring to stay at the shortest end of the yield curve and remain cautious about longer-duration bonds amid long-term inflation concerns. Even the Oracle of Omaha has accumulated a record amount of cash, most of which is invested in Treasury bills.

Investors should remember that as interest rates rise, bond prices fall, unless they invest in individual bonds and hold them to maturity. A recent Wall Street Journal survey indicated that economists expect interest rates to remain elevated for an extended period.

While stock-bond correlations have risen sharply over the past few years, cash and ultra-short-term bonds maintain virtually zero correlation with equities, offering meaningful diversification benefits to a portfolio.

Money Market ETFs: What Investors Should Know

This ETF category has attracted significant interest since Texas Capital launched the first money market ETF. Lower expense ratios compared with mutual funds and investors' preference for the ETF structure have helped drive demand. BlackRock, JPMorgan, and other providers have followed with their own money market ETFs.

Most money market mutual funds are required to maintain a net asset value (NAV) of $1 per share. Although their share prices do not appreciate, investors receive regular dividends, allowing their investments to grow over time.

Unlike traditional money market mutual funds, money market ETFs typically have fluctuating share prices and often launch with a NAV of around $100. Their NAVs may fluctuate slightly due to market demand, bid-ask spreads, and changes in underlying yields, but they generally remain close to their initial NAVs.

Government money market funds invest in Treasury bills and government agency securities, including those issued by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Prime money market funds invest in a mix of corporate and government securities.

Municipal money market funds are particularly appealing to high-income investors because the interest earned is generally exempt from federal income tax and may also be exempt from state income tax.

title: Tech Stocks Are Crushing the Market, but There's a Sneaky (and Dangerous) Risk for S&P 500 Investors
detail:
Tech Stocks Are Crushing the Market, but There's a Sneaky (and Dangerous) Risk for S&P 500 Investors
Bram Berkowitz, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 11:13 AM MDT 5 min read
NVDA
^GSPC
QQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Many market strategists have expressed concern about tech and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, believing many of them are either overvalued or overearning amid an AI supercycle that may not be sustainable.

But investors who have owned large tech and AI stocks have likely done well in recent years. The Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index, is up 108% in the past five years, soundly outperforming the broader benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) index's nearly 78% rise in the same time frame.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Although the S&P 500 is often considered safer than investing solely in tech stocks, there's a sneaky -- and potentially dangerous -- risk investors should be aware of.

Image source: Getty Images.
Nowhere to hide

The S&P 500 is intended to reflect the broader stock market. It's a market-weighted index, so when companies in it grow, they receive more weight in the index.

In recent years, many large tech and AI names have surpassed a $1 trillion market cap or even become multitrillion-dollar companies. As such, they now account for a large share of the S&P 500. Here are the 10 largest names in the index by their respective weightings:

Nvidia -- 7.8%

Apple -- 6.9%

Microsoft -- 5.6%

Amazon -- 4.0%

Alphabet (Class A) -- 3.1%

Alphabet (Class C) -- 2.9%

Meta Platforms -- 2.6%

Broadcom -- 2.4%

Tesla -- 2.1%

Micron Technology -- 1.6%

Combined, these 10 names now make up about 39% of the S&P 500. Whether investors signed up for it or not, if they own the S&P 500, they have a much larger stake in big tech than in previous years.

In recent years, big tech became not only a growth play to capitalize on AI but also a flight-to-safety bet, with the belief that these companies were too systemically important and generated too much cash to ever face a serious threat.

However, many of them have now invested hundreds of billions in AI-related infrastructure, such as data centers, and several are now experiencing negative free cash flow. While AI looks like a total game changer, there's still no guarantee that these huge capital investments will pay off.

The big risk is that if the AI trade softens, these stocks could get hammered, potentially taking the market with it. Previously, investing in the S&P 500 provided much more diversification for long-term investors.

The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (BATS:IGV) shows the swing. It rose 41.46% from April 13 through October 12, 2026, and closed at $111.31.

That beat the 20.84% gain in the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) and the 13.41% gain in the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) over the same period.

Investors who sold near the April low missed that rebound, and anyone looking at the fund now faces a harder decision. The open question is the balance. How much of this reflects a lasting re-rating of software, and how much reflects a crowded momentum trade that has already done most of its work.

IGV's Six-Month Surge Hides a Losing Year

Over longer time frames, the picture is weaker: over one year, IGV is down 0.68%, and year-to-date it is up only 5.34%. A fund can lead the market for six months and still trade below where it stood a year ago, which makes the April rally a recovery of earlier losses.

The past month added 9.64%. But the fund fell 1.21% in the October 12 session. So the advance has had pauses along the way, and anyone who bought a year ago has spent twelve months getting back to roughly even.

Micron slides 5% on direct CXMT server memory competition; SanDisk drops 4% on sector sentiment despite having zero server memory exposure.

The Roundhill Memory ETF falls 5% while QQQ loses just 1%, showing how sharply the CXMT threat concentrates pain on memory stocks.

CXMT's president announced a denser server memory chip launching by year-end at a Shanghai conference, threatening pricing across the entire high-end segment.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Micron Technology didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat MU. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Memory stocks are slipping for a second straight session after Chinese rival CXMT laid out plans to compete for the high-end server market. Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) stock is at $942.21, down 5% in morning trading, with the selloff landing directly on its core server memory business. The damage is landing hardest where a new rival's product would compete head-on.

Vitalii Stock / Shutterstock.com

Meanwhile, SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock is at $1,421.78, down 4%, a slightly smaller drop for a flash storage company with no server memory line. That near match is the puzzle this selloff poses, since only one of the two sells the product CXMT is targeting.

To gauge how concentrated the damage is, the Roundhill Memory ETF (CBOE:DRAM) serves as a sector proxy, and it's at $51.73, down 5%. By comparison, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $741.01, down 0.7%, a much softer decline for the broad tech market.

CXMT Plans a Push Into High-End Server Memory

CXMT, which is privately held, said over the weekend that it plans to launch a denser server memory product by the end of this year. Its president announced the plan at a chip conference in Shanghai. The design packs more cells into the same chip area. That step would move CXMT into the high-end server memory market the established suppliers hold.

Burry sold his Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac common shares and shifted into junior preferred shares, which now make up about 8%-10% of his portfolio.

He sees potential four-to-fivefold upside in the preferreds if the government resolves its senior claims and reinstates dividends.

"The Big Short" investor Michael Burry sees a possible "bull trap" in stocks at new highs but is holding back on adding shorts, while his 8%-10% portfolio bet on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred shares depends on a government resolution.

His warning came after a mixed Monday session: the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) slipped 0.06%, the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) fell 0.7%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) gained 0.35%, while the S&P 500 hovered near its record high set the previous week.

Burry Keeps Bearish Bets In Puts

"The market is not so conducive right now," Burry said in a Substack chat. "Lots of these stocks, you have to respect the new highs. Might be a bull trap, and a number of big bear markets have started that way." His challenge, he said, is staying positioned until his view plays out: "I just know where this will be in a few years. The trick is to get there."

Burry added that Puts account for about 10% of his portfolio. Long positions and LEAPS make up most of the rest, with minimal cash. "If the market crashes hard, I think I'll do ok," he said, adding that he expects his long holdings to perform over three to five years. "A year is nothing."

Why Burry Prefers Fannie and Freddie's Junior Shares

Burry's reluctance to add shorts does not mean he has dropped his bearish bets. In his most recent Substack post, he said almost all his short exposure was expressed through puts on the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor stocks. The options expire in 2027 and were 20% out of the money. He put his window for a significant market top at zero to nine months.

Burry sold his Fannie and Freddie common shares and added them to junior preferred stock (JPS). When asked how he moved from Fannie common into Freddie common and then out of both, he replied: "Almost as soon as I dumped the Fannie into Freddie, I was not comfortable with my risk position and started moving all and then some into the JPS."

The preferred shares rank above common stock in the capital structure. Burry's thesis is that they could benefit if the government resolves its senior claims and reinstates preferred dividends. He said the junior preferreds could trade well above par depending on interest rates, adding that the potential return "from current levels" could reach four to five times.
